Hybrid RAS shells were fabricated in 'C' and 'U' shapes using glass fiber/epoxy/carbon-black absorbing layers and carbon fiber epoxy reflection layers.
Carbon-black nanoparticles used had an average diameter of 40 nm and a surface area of 950 cm²/g.
The carbon-black content in the absorbing layer was 5 wt%, selected based on previous studies.
Sixteen plies of GFRP-CB prepreg were laid at the bottom, and eight plies of CFRP prepreg were laid on top during fabrication.
Aluminum molds with additional bending angles were used to compensate for spring-back deformation during curing.
The curing cycle was 2 hours at 120°C and 5.5 atm in an autoclave.
Spring-back compensation achieved zero spring-back at mold bending angles of -4.29° for 'C' shape and -1.9° for 'U' shape shells.
Finite element analysis using ANSYS predicted spring-back angles with about 21.8% average error compared to experiments.
The reflection coefficient of CFRP was about 120 dB, considered as a perfect electric conductor (PEC) in this study.
Radar cross section (RCS) was measured at 10 GHz using a compact range method.
The hybrid RAS shells showed an average radar absorption efficiency of approximately 11 dB compared to PEC shells.
The physical optics method was used to predict RCS and showed good agreement with experimental results (errors <7%).
The RCS reduction of 11 dB corresponds to a significant decrease in reflected radar signal intensity.
The study used Stratton-Chu equations and closed-form expressions to calculate RCS for simple geometries.
The hybrid RAS structure combines electromagnetic wave absorption and high structural stiffness.
The spring-back effect is caused by thermal mismatch and chemical shrinkage during curing of thermoset composites.
Mechanical properties used in simulation: GFRP-CB elastic modulus 20.8 GPa, CFRP elastic modulus 81.2 GPa.
Thermal expansion coefficients: GFRP-CB ~8.5e-6 /°C, CFRP ~-1.54e-6 /°C.
The fabricated shells maintained dimensional accuracy by fixing molds with jigs during curing.
The study demonstrated the feasibility of fabricating complex 3D radar absorbing composite shells with controlled dimensional fidelity.
